claims.claim: Siepmann's 2017 corpus study: the impression of archaicity comes from overuse of nineteenth-century fiction words (yonder, journey (v), topmost), avoidance of modern-world words, and dense use of coinages, unusual patterns and obsolescent words; reference corpora were 30m (19th-c fiction), 160m (post-war fiction) and 94m (mixed).
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist: a corpus-based investigation' (Corpus Linguistics 2017, Birmingham)

claims.claim: Modern key words (they, big, wake, wall, tired, smoke) are used in nineteenth-century patterns, e.g. 'a black smoke' with indefinite article, rare in modern fiction.
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist: a corpus-based investigation' (Corpus Linguistics 2017, Birmingham)

claims.claim: Wikipedia cites Turner: Tolkien's style is generally simple parataxis, varied by the race and standing of the speaker; at Pelennor the paratactic repeated 'and' creates an exalted biblical register with few archaic words.

Wikipedia cites Shippey's 'loose semantic fit' (conjunctions avoiding explicit logical connection) at significant moments and Rosebury on inversion working better than the plain order ('But glad would he have been').

McIntosh, citing Garth (p. 271), describes Tolkien's parataxis as short simple sentences joined by 'and' in the Ride of the Rohirrim and Pelennor, producing breathless excitement and rising foreboding.
claims.source: Jonathan McIntosh, 'Tolkien's use of parataxis', The Flame Imperishable (2012)

claims.claim: Thomas (per Nepveu): The Hobbit opens with a very intrusive narrator who recedes as the book grows serious; the LOTR narrator is impartial and self-effacing, and early LOTR drafts were unsuccessful returns to the intrusive voice (Booth's scale).
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, summary of Paul Edmund Thomas, 'Some of Tolkien's Narrators' (2000)

claims.claim: Poveda: The Hobbit's narrator is omniscient, comments on events, addresses the reader as a child, withholds and anticipates information, and is conscious of the written medium.
claims.source: Jaume Albero Poveda, 'Narrative models in Tolkien's stories of Middle-earth', Journal of English Studies 4 (2003-04)

claims.claim: Poveda: LOTR begins in a conversational tone with Hobbit-style asides and an occasionally unreliable narrator ('probably started by the knowledgeable Sam'), but as the plot progresses the voice becomes neutral and the narrator disappears behind the characters.
claims.source: Jaume Albero Poveda, 'Narrative models in Tolkien's stories of Middle-earth', Journal of English Studies 4 (2003-04)
claims.quote: the narrator disappears behind the characters

claims.feature: archaic style confined to elf/men episodes
claims.claim: Poveda: archaic forms (ye, hath) and noun-adjective inversion are not predominant but confined to episodes of Elves and Men inspired by epic, chiefly Books II and III; capitalised common nouns (the Sea, the City) mark the style.
claims.source: Jaume Albero Poveda, 'Narrative models in Tolkien's stories of Middle-earth', Journal of English Studies 4 (2003-04)

claims.claim: Litschko, using Stanzel and Booth, characterises The Hobbit's narrator as an intrusive authorial narrator who comments and judges, addresses readers directly, shifts point of view, and changes tone in the later-written final chapters.
claims.source: Nadja Litschko, 'The Voice of the Narrator in J.R.R. Tolkien's The Hobbit' (GRIN, 2006)

claims.feature: limited omniscience when no hobbit present
claims.claim: aefenglommung: the story is seen mainly through Frodo's mind, occasionally Merry or Pippin, and increasingly Sam; where no hobbit is present Tolkien draws back into limited omniscience and we do not enter Aragorn's, Gimli's or Legolas's minds, Book 3 reading like a stage-play.
claims.quote: we do not enter their minds

claims.feature: multiple tellers and limited vs omniscient narrators
claims.claim: Barkley compares the versions of tales told by Bilbo, Aragorn, Gandalf, the Red Book's scholar-editor and the Silmarillion's omniscient narrator: the limited narrator is narrower in scope but richer in detail, dialogue and song, the omniscient broader in theme.
claims.source: Christine Barkley, 'Point of View in Tolkien', Mythlore 21.2 (1996)
claims.quote: The limited third-person narrative focuses attention more on one character

claims.claim: Barkley: the Prologue's Red Book of Westmarch frame authenticates the tale, gives away the happy ending, and contrasts with The Hobbit, whose narrator paraphrased Bilbo's account and revealed his own bias.
claims.source: Christine Barkley, 'Point of View in Tolkien', Mythlore 21.2 (1996)

claims.claim: Wikipedia cites Thomson (1967) and Turner (2011) for the found-manuscript frame in which Tolkien poses as editor/translator of the Red Book, with genealogies and footnotes as editorial apparatus.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Storytelling in The Lord of the Rings

claims.claim: Tauber: The Hobbit's 19 chapters (70th Anniversary edition) yield 95,137 whitespace tokens in 11,532 types, or 95,390/95,643 depending on em-dash handling; 5,165 types carry trailing punctuation and 254 contain em-dashes.
claims.source: James Tauber, 'Tokenizing the Hobbit' (Digital Tolkien Project, 2021)

verdicts.trueWording: the impression of archaicity ... is partly due to three simple lexical causes
verdicts.note: Raw PDF fetched live (200, 4pp, pdfminer text). Quote 'three simple lexical causes' verbatim. All three causes verbatim: 'overuse' of words borrowed from nineteenth-century fiction, avoidance of words associated with the modern world, dense use of new coinages, unusual grammatical patterns, rare or obsolescent words. yonder, journey (v) and topmost all appear in the listed 19th-century key words. Corpora verbatim: 19th-century corpus 'about 30 million words', post-war fiction 'around 160 million running words', 'a reference corpus of 94 million words' (heterogeneous/mixed). Only softening: the page says 'partly due to', the claim says 'comes from'.

verdicts.trueWording: Tolkien tends to use many of these words in nineteenth-century patterns
verdicts.note: No quotation supplied, so VERBATIM is not assessable; every limb is on the raw page, mostly word for word: modern key words 'such as they, big, wake, wall, unfriendly, tired or smoke'; smoke 'commonly preceded by the indefinite article in Lord of the Rings (e.g. ... a black smoke swirled in the air.), a use that is notably infrequent in modern fiction'. The page's list also includes 'unfriendly', which the claim omits (an omission, not an error).

verdicts.trueWording: the paratactic style here, with the repeated use of "and" in the manner of the New Testament
verdicts.note: Raw Wikipedia HTML fetched (200) and de-tagged. Quote 'repeated use of "and"' verbatim. Turner limb verbatim: 'Tolkien's style is both generally simple, using parataxis ... and varied, adapted to the race and standing of the speaker'. Pelennor limb verbatim: Turner on the second eucatastrophe in the Battle of the Pelennor Fields, readers experience 'an impression of exalted register' because of the biblical association, 'even though Tolkien uses few unusual or archaic words in the passage'.

verdicts.trueWording: Shippey calls such deliberate use of the conjunction, avoiding explicit logical connection, "loose semantic fit"
verdicts.note: No quotation supplied, so VERBATIM is not assessable; both limbs are on the raw page in the claim's own words. Shippey limb sits in the Pelennor eucatastrophe passage (the article separately credits Turner with 'special stylistic effects at key moments'). Rosebury limb verbatim: 'the following "But glad would he have been", with effective use of inversion. Rosebury shows how awkward the uninverted form would have been: "But he who wrought it long ago ... would have been glad to know its fate."'

verdicts.trueWording: using it to achieve a sense of "breathless excitement"
verdicts.note: Raw WordPress page fetched (200). Quote word for word apart from the source's internal quotation marks around 'breathless excitement'. Garth attribution and page verbatim: '(Tolkien and the Great War, 271)'. Parataxis defined as 'short, simple sentences joined by coordinating conjunctions (e.g., "and")'. Both examples are from 'The Ride of the Rohirrim' and 'The Battle of Pelennor Fields'. 'Rising foreboding' corresponds to the page's 'cranking up the tension and foreboding before the denouement'.

verdicts.trueWording: the narrator has become impartial and self-effacing
verdicts.note: Raw LiveJournal HTML fetched (200), post dated June 6 2006. Quote verbatim. Every limb verbatim: 'the opening of The Hobbit is told by a very intrusive narrator, but as the book gets more serious toward the end, the narrator recedes'; 'the initial drafts of LotR, which were unsuccessful attempts to return to the intrusive voice'; Booth footnote: 'a system from Wayne Booth's The Rhetoric of Fiction that characterizes narrators on a scale between unintrusive and intrusive'.

verdicts.trueWording: omniscient, frequently discusses the events, speaks to the reader as if to a child
verdicts.note: Raw PDF fetched live from Dialnet (200, 16pp) and text-extracted. No quotation supplied. All limbs supported: omniscient and 'constantly speaks to the reader as if to a child'; 'deliberately conceals pieces of information in order to generate interest' and 'omits data that the reader already knows' (withholding); anticipation via 'you will see whether he gained anything in the end' and postponing to 'the next chapter'; 'he is conscious of the fact that his narration is in a written medium'. Kuznets is also cited on the page for 'an omniscient narrator that comments on events and addresses the reader directly'.

verdicts.trueWording: the narrative voice becomes more neutral and the narrator disappears behind the characters
verdicts.note: Same raw Dialnet PDF. Quote 'the narrator disappears behind the characters' verbatim. Limbs verbatim: 'It begins with a chapter that has a conversational and uninhibited tone'; 'some of the asides that also characterize the narrative voice of The Hobbit'; 'The narrator is sometimes unreliable: "A day or two later a rumour (probably started by the knowledgeable Sam)" (I, 47)'. Page reads 'more neutral'; claim says 'neutral'.

verdicts.trueWording: the archaic style is not predominant throughout the story ... (chiefly books II and III)
verdicts.note: Same raw Dialnet PDF. Quote 'chiefly books II and III' verbatim. Limbs verbatim: 'the use of archaic forms such as "ye" and "hath" and the inversion of nouns and adjectives'; 'used in episodes relating to the world of elves and men -in short, those inspired by epic fantasy'; 'creating proper names by using a capital letter for the first letter of common nouns ... the Sea, the City, the Gate'. Poveda judges the capitals a flaw ('makes the style pompous'), which the claim's neutral 'mark the style' does not contradict.

verdicts.trueWording: the narrator of The Hobbit is an intrusive authorial narrator who frequently comments on and judges
verdicts.note: Raw GRIN product page fetched (200); it carries the paper's summary, ToC, abstract and an excerpt. Quote 'intrusive authorial narrator' verbatim, in: 'an intrusive authorial narrator who frequently comments on and judges the characters as well as the unfolding events ... and who addressed his readers in a direct way'. Stanzel/Booth limb: 'Analysis of narrative situations based on the theories of Franz K. Stanzel and Wayne C. Booth'. Point-of-view limb is ToC section 2.3.6 'Changing the Point of View'. Final-chapters limb: 'changes to the narrative voice in the last chapters of the book, which were written over three years after the rest of the novel'. Author/year/venue on page: Nadja Litschko, 2006, GRIN.

verdicts.trueWording: Tolkien tends to draw back into a limited omniscience ... we do not enter their minds
verdicts.note: Raw LiveJournal HTML fetched (200), post dated September 14 2021. Quote 'we do not enter their minds' verbatim, and it appears twice. Limbs verbatim: 'We see this story mainly through Frodo's mind. As the story develops, we occasionally enter Merry or Pippin's mind. Toward the end, we see a lot of the story through Sam's mind'; Book 3 on Aragorn, Legolas and Gimli 'Tolkien reverts to limited omniscience ... we do not enter their minds'; and, in the same Book 3 discussion, 'we are witnessing all this like those watching a stage-play'.

verdicts.trueWording: The limited third-person narrative focuses attention more on one character
verdicts.note: The dc.swosu.edu landing page carries only an abstract; the article PDF (viewcontent.cgi?article=2155) returns 403 to a browser UA live, so recovered via the Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/20230512031427id_/... (200, application/pdf, 18pp) and text-extracted. Quote verbatim (line-wrapped in the PDF). Tellers list verbatim: 'Bilbo, Aragorn, Gandalf, the historian/scholar who discovered the "Red Book of Westmarch", the scribe in Minas Tirith who recorded Aragorn's story, and the omniscient narrator in The Silmarillion'. Contrast verbatim: 'the more limited point of view is less broad in scope or theme, but at least in Tolkien more detailed in description, dialogue, poetry, song, etc. The omniscient narrator has a broader purpose'.

verdicts.trueWording: frame tale which authenticates the story ... and gives away the "happy ending"
verdicts.note: Same Wayback raw PDF of the Mythlore article. No quotation supplied. All limbs on the page: 'the entire frame tale which authenticates the story as having come from the "Red Book of Westmarch" ... also provides a larger context for the present tale and gives away the "happy ending" by mentioning some history of the characters after the events of the present tale. This level is useful to compare with the point of view in The Hobbit, as well, since the narrator then paraphrased Bilbo's account, revealing his own bias.'

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that Wikipedia cites Thomson (1967) for the found-manuscript / editor-translator frame - Thomson [9] is cited only in the 'traditional romance' section (tapestry romance, Frye's phases); the framing paragraph cites [12] Turner 2011a and [14] Brljak 2010, and the following sentence [12][13][14][15]
verdicts.trueWording: found manuscript conceit ... he was the book's editor and translator (cited to Turner 2011a, Brljak 2010)
verdicts.note: Raw Wikipedia HTML fetched (200) and de-tagged; citation numbers resolved against the article's own Secondary reference list, in which Thomson 1967 is note 9 and Turner 2011a is note 12. The rest of the claim is supported: 'The found manuscript conceit, and the claim that he had translated it into English from the original Westron rather than written it himself, put him in the frame with the story that he was the book's editor and translator'; the Red Book frame at 'Tolkien came up with a frame story for the sequel, the Red Book of Westmarch'; and the lead's 'many other elements such as genealogies and footnotes, giving the impression that Tolkien was the editor and translator of the work, forming an editorial frame'. Only the Thomson attribution fails.

verdicts.trueWording: The 95,137 tokens come in 11,532 different types
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (200). The supplied quotation '95,137 tokens in 11,532 types' is NOT on the page word for word: the page has 'we get 95,137 tokens in The Hobbit' and, separately, 'The 95,137 tokens come in 11,532 different types'. Every figure checks out: 70th Anniversary edition; 'just deal with the 19 chapters of the main narrative'; whitespace split gives 95,137; 'we've suggested 95,137, 95,390 and 95,643 as possibilities' turning on em-dash handling; '5,165 types consist of a word followed by punctuation'; and the residual '254 remaining types that have an em-dash in the middle' ('These all have em-dashes in them').
